q: A camera is an optical instrument that forms and records an image of an object.
e: True. A camera forms and records an image of an object on film or on an electronic sensor. A convex lens throws a real inverted image onto that screen. Magnetic or thermal sensors are not the usual picture-taker.

q: The image may be recorded on film or it may be detected by an electronic sensor that stores the image analogously.
e: False. An electronic sensor stores the image digitally, as pixels, not analogously. Film is the chemical analogue record. Digital cameras replaced that film with a pixel array.

q: A convex lens focuses the light from the object to form a real inverted image on the film or electronic sensor.
e: True. A concave lens diverges and will not form that real film image. Focusing then slides the lens distance until the image is sharp. The camera's convex lens converges light to a real inverted image on the film or sensor.

q: A diaphragm is placed in front of the convex lens to control the amount of light energy falling on the film.
e: False. The diaphragm is placed behind the convex lens to control how much light hits the film. In front would be the wrong side of the focusing element. Amount of light is its job; time is the shutter's job.

q: The aperture is a circular opening through which the light passes.
e: True. Bright light wants a large f-number; dim light wants a small one. Aperture is the circular opening light passes through. f-number is focal length over diameter; smaller f-number means a wider hole.

q: The size or the diameter of the aperture is expressed in terms of f-numbers.
e: True. Small f-number, wide aperture, more light. Bright scenes need a large f-number so the hole is stopped down. f-number is focal length of the lens divided by aperture diameter.

q: The f-number of a camera is the ratio of the diameter of aperture to the focal length of the lens.
e: False. f-number is focal length divided by aperture diameter, f/D, not D/f. A small f-number is a wide hole. Bright light wants a large f-number so the hole is stopped down.

q: The smaller the f-number, the wider the aperture is.
e: True. f-number is focal length of the lens divided by aperture diameter. Small f-number, wide aperture, more light. Bright scenes need a large f-number so the hole is stopped down.

q: When taking a photograph in bright light a small f-number (wide aperture) must be used.
e: False. Bright light needs a large f-number, meaning a narrow aperture, so the film is not flooded. Small f-number, wide aperture, is for dim light. The diaphragm is how you make that change.

q: When taking a photograph in dim light a small f-number (wide aperture) must be used.
e: True. Bright scenes need a large f-number so the hole is stopped down. f-number is focal length of the lens divided by aperture diameter. Small f-number, wide aperture, more light.

q: A shutter controls the time during which light enters the camera through the lens.
e: True. The shutter controls how long light may enter through the lens. Shutter speed is quoted as that exposure time. Shorter exposure is a higher shutter speed; focal length is a different knob.

q: The shutter speed is expressed in terms of the focal length.
e: False. Shutter speed is quoted as exposure time, not as focal length. Focal length belongs to the lens and to the f-number. Short exposure is a high shutter speed.

q: The shorter the exposure time, the higher the shutter speed is.
e: True. The shutter times how long light may enter through the lens. Shutter speed is quoted as that exposure time. A short exposure is a high shutter speed; focal length is a different control.

q: A camera consists of a focusing ring by which the distance between the lens and the film can be adjusted to obtain a sharp image on the film.
e: True. It is not a brightness control. Wrong distance leaves the picture blurred. The focusing ring changes lens-to-film distance until the image is sharp.

q: The film consists of a thin layer of chemical compounds of gold.
e: False. Photographic film uses silver compounds, not gold. Those silver grains blacken where light hits. Digital sensors then replace the whole chemical layer with pixels.

q: In a digital camera, the film is replaced by an electronic sensor made up of millions of tiny pixels which response to light.
e: True. Diodes or grains are not the name of those picture elements. A digital sensor is millions of tiny pixels that respond to light. They store the image digitally, not analogously.

q: Human eye consists of sense organs which are capable of receiving visual images and sending the information to the brain.
e: True. The brain interprets that picture as upright. The eye receives visual images and sends them to the brain along the optic nerve. The retinal image is real, inverted and smaller than the object.

q: The front portion of the eye is covered by a tough, opaque membrane called the cornea.
e: False. The cornea is a tough transparent membrane at the front of the eye. Opaque would block the image before it started. Light has to enter there.

q: The region between the cornea and the eyelens is filled with a transparent liquid called the aqueous humour.
e: True. Aqueous humour is the transparent liquid between cornea and eyelens. Vitreous humour fills the larger chamber between eyelens and retina. Those two jellies are not interchangeable.

q: The region between the eyelens and the retina contains a transparent liquid called the aqueous humour.
e: False. Between eyelens and retina sits vitreous humour. Aqueous humour fills the front chamber between cornea and lens. Swap those names and you have put the jelly in the wrong room.

q: The iris which is the colored portion of the eye controls the amount of light energy entering the eye.
e: True. The pupil dilates in dim light and contracts in bright light. The iris is the coloured part of the eye and controls how much light enters. The pupil is the hole in its centre, the eye's aperture.

q: The pupil is in the centre of the iris and the light passes through it.
e: True. The pupil dilates in dim light and contracts in bright light. The iris is the coloured part of the eye and controls how much light enters. Pupil is in the centre of the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The pupil automatically contracts in dim light and dilates in bright light.
e: False. The pupil dilates in dim light and contracts in bright light. That is the iris working as the camera aperture. The wrong way round would dazzle you in sun and starve you in shade.

q: The ciliary muscles are attached to the eyelens.
e: True. Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex. For distant objects they relax and the lens flattens.

q: The ciliary muscles can vary the thickness of the eyelens, thus alter the focal length of the lens to obtain a sharp image on the retina.
e: True. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex. For distant objects they relax and the lens flattens. Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length.

q: When near objects are viewed, the ciliary muscles relax and permit the eyelens to form a less convex shape.
e: False. For a near object the ciliary muscles contract and the eyelens becomes more convex. Relaxation and a flatter lens are for distant objects. Accommodation is that thickness change.

q: When distant objects are viewed, the ciliary muscles relax and the eyelens becomes less convex.
e: True. For distant objects they relax and the lens flattens. Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex.

q: The retina is the light sensitive area of the cells, at the back of the eye.
e: True. The image there is real, inverted and smaller than the object. The optic nerve then carries that signal to the brain. The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, with rods and cones.

q: The retina consists of rods and cones.
e: True. The yellow spot is cone-packed and most sensitive for fine detail. The blind spot has no rods or cones, where the optic nerve leaves. The retina at the back of the eye holds rods and cones.

q: The yellow spot which is the least light-sensitive spot on the retina is used for viewing very small objects.
e: False. The yellow spot is the most light-sensitive region and is packed with cones. The blind spot is the insensitive patch with no rods or cones. Fine detail is a yellow-spot job.

q: The yellow spot consists of cones exclusively.
e: True. yellow and spot have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of yellow would describe a different law.

q: There is a spot on the retina which has no rods or cones called the blind spot.
e: True. The blind spot has no rods or cones, where the optic nerve leaves. The retina at the back of the eye holds rods and cones. The yellow spot is cone-packed and most sensitive for fine detail.

q: The light energy falling on the retina is transmitted to the brain by the ciliary nerve.
e: False. The optic nerve carries the retinal signal to the brain. Ciliary muscles only squeeze the lens. Nerve and muscle are different jobs.

q: The cornea, the aqueous humour, the eyelens and the vitreous humour are refracting substances.
e: True. Opaque would block the image at the door. Aqueous humour then fills the chamber behind it, before the eyelens. Aqueous humour is the transparent liquid between cornea and eyelens.

q: The image of an object formed on the retina by these four substances is virtual, erect and smaller than the size of the object.
e: False. The retinal image is real, inverted, and smaller than the object. The brain reads that inverted picture as upright. Virtual erect images belong to simple magnifiers, not to the retina.

q: Farsightedness is a defect of vision in which distant objects are seen clearly, but objects nearby are blurry.
e: True. Farsightedness, hyperopia: distant objects are clear, nearby ones are blurry. Near rays meet behind the retina, so a converging convex lens is the correction. A diverging lens is the myopia tool, not this one.

q: Nearsightedness is a defect of vision in which near objects are seen clearly, but objects far away are blurry.
e: True. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Nearsightedness, myopia: near objects are clear, distant ones are blurry.

q: For a person with farsightedness, the rays from near objects intersect at a point in front of the retina after passing through the eyelens.
e: False. In farsightedness, near rays meet behind the retina. In front of the retina is the myopia meeting point for distant rays. Convex spectacles add the extra convergence hyperopia needs.

q: Farsightedness is due to an eyeball which is too short or due to the eyelens which cannot be sufficiently convex.
e: True. Farsightedness, hyperopia: distant objects are clear, nearby ones are blurry. Near rays meet behind the retina, so a converging convex lens is the correction. Farsightedness is due to an eyeball which cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Farsightedness can be corrected by the use of spectacles with diverging lens or concave lens.
e: False. Farsightedness needs a converging convex lens. A diverging concave lens is the myopia correction. Hyperopia is not enough bending; you add a convex lens, you do not take bending away.

q: For a person with nearsightedness, the rays from distant objects intersect at a point in front of the retina after passing through the eyelens.
e: True. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Person with nearsightedness the rays from distant cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Nearsightedness is due to an eyeball which is too long or due to the eyelens which is more convex than is necessary.
e: True. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Nearsightedness is due to an eyeball which cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Nearsightedness can be corrected by the use of spectacles with converging lens or convex lens.
e: False. Nearsightedness needs a diverging concave lens so distant rays meet on the retina, not in front of it. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Myopia and hyperopia take opposite spectacles.

q: For normal vision the least distance of distinct vision is about $25	ext{ cm}$.
e: True. The far point for normal vision is infinity. Least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm for a normal eye. Nearer than that, the lens cannot bulge enough.

q: For normal vision the maximum distance of distinct vision is infinity.
e: True. Half-integer path difference is a minimum. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima.

q: A microscope is an optical instrument which uses lenses to make enlarged images of objects that are too small for the unaided eye to see.
e: True. A compound microscope uses two convex lenses to enlarge a nearby tiny object. The object sits just outside the objective's focus, and total magnifying power is a product, not a sum. The objective should have the shorter focal length.

q: A compound microscope has at least two concave lenses: an objective lens and an eyepiece lens.
e: False. A compound microscope uses convex lenses, at least an objective and an eyepiece. Concave lenses diverge and will not build those real magnified images. Both stages are converging.

q: The lens nearer the object is called the objective and the lens through which the final image is viewed is called the eyepiece.
e: True. In a microscope it is short-focus and throws a real magnified image. In an astronomical telescope it is long-focus and wide for light gathering. The eyepiece is the lens toward the eye and adds angular magnification.

q: When the compound microscope is used, the object should be placed beyond $2F$, where $F$ is the focus of the objective.
e: False. For a compound microscope the object sits just outside the objective's focal point, between F and 2F, not beyond 2F. Beyond 2F you get a diminished real image, which is the wrong start. The objective must magnify.

q: The objective produces an image which is real, inverted and larger than the size of the object.
e: True. In an astronomical telescope it is long-focus and wide for light gathering. The objective is the lens toward the object. In a microscope it is short-focus and throws a real magnified image.

q: The eyepiece acts as a magnifying glass to view this image and the final image formed is virtual and on the same side as the object.
e: True. Telescope magnifying power wants this eyepiece short compared with the objective. The eyepiece is the lens toward the eye and adds angular magnification. Microscope magnifying power multiplies objective and eyepiece factors.

q: The magnifying power (MP) of a compound microscope is the sum of the magnification of the objective and the magnifying power of the eyepiece.
e: False. Magnifying power of a compound microscope is a product, M_objective times M_eyepiece, not a sum. Each stage multiplies the previous size. Adding the two numbers undercounts the enlargement.

q: For a large magnifying power of a compound microscope both the objective and the eyepiece should have short focal lengths.
e: True. The objective should have a shorter focal length than the eyepiece. A compound microscope uses at least two convex lenses to enlarge a nearby tiny object. The object sits just outside the objective's focus, and magnifying power is a product of the two stages.

q: The focal length of the objective should be longer than that of the eyepiece.
e: False. In a compound microscope the objective should have a shorter focal length than the eyepiece, so the first image is strongly magnified. A long-focus objective is the telescope choice. Microscope and telescope swap that ratio.

q: As the magnifying power increases, the sharpness of images is reduced.
e: True. magnifying and power have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of magnifying would describe a different law.

q: Electron microscope is a microscope with high magnification and resolution, employing electron beams in place of light and using electron lenses.
e: True. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. An electron microscope uses an electron beam and electron lenses instead of light and glass. Shorter electron wavelength gives higher magnification and resolution.

q: Optical microscopes use simple lenses, whereas electron microscopes use electrostatic or electromagnetic lenses.
e: True. Shorter electron wavelength gives higher magnification and resolution. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. An electron microscope uses an electron beam and electron lenses instead of light and glass.

q: Optical microscopes use electrons, while electron microscopes use photons or light energy, which have shorter wavelengths that allows greater magnification.
e: False. Optical microscopes use light, photons; electron microscopes use electrons. The electron's shorter wavelength is why EM resolution is higher. The statement has the particles backwards.

q: In an electron microscope, a beam of accelerated electrons is used as a source of illumination.
e: True. Shorter electron wavelength gives higher magnification and resolution. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. Electron microscope a beam of accelerated electrons cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: There are two main types of electron microscope: the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM).
e: True. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. An electron microscope uses an electron beam and electron lenses instead of light and glass. Two main types of electron microscope the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The accelerated electron beam is focused by simple glass lenses, and transmitted through the specimen.
e: False. An electron beam is focused by electron lenses, magnetic or electric, not by simple glass. Glass is for photons. The specimen still sits in the beam, but the optics are electron optics.

q: The image of the specimen may be viewed by projecting the magnified electron image onto a fluorescent viewing screen.
e: True. image and specimen have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of image would describe a different law.

q: An optical instrument used for viewing distant objects is called a telescope.
e: True. The final image for a relaxed eye is virtual, inverted and magnified. A wide objective gathers light and improves resolution. A refracting astronomical telescope wants a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece.

q: The refracting astronomical telescope consists of an objective of short focal length and an eyepiece of long focal length.
e: False. An astronomical refractor wants a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece. That ratio is the magnifying power. Short objective plus long eyepiece would minify the heavens.

q: Both lenses in a refracting astronomical telescope are convex lenses.
e: True. A refracting astronomical telescope has a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece. The final image for a relaxed eye is virtual, inverted and magnified. A large objective diameter gathers light and sharpens resolution.

q: A real and inverted image of a distant object is formed at the focus of the objective.
e: True. The objective is the lens toward the object. In a microscope it is short-focus and throws a real magnified image. In an astronomical telescope it is long-focus and wide for light gathering.

q: The final image formed by the eyepiece is real, smaller than the first image and erect with respect to the distant object.
e: False. The eyepiece of an astronomical telescope forms a virtual, magnified, inverted image of the distant object. Real, smaller, and erect is not that telescope image.

q: For a high magnifying power of the refracting astronomical telescope, an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length are required.
e: True. A large objective diameter gathers light and sharpens resolution. A refracting astronomical telescope has a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece. The final image for a relaxed eye is virtual, inverted and magnified.

q: To obtain the sharp images of distant objects the objective should have a small diameter.
e: False. A large objective diameter gathers more light and improves resolution of distant objects. Small diameter starves the image. Sharp, bright astronomy wants a wide objective.

q: In practice, a concave mirror instead of a convex lens is used as an objective in most telescopes used at the astronomical observatories.
e: True. A convex lens converges light and can form a real inverted image. Cameras, microscope objectives and the eyelens for near vision all use extra converging power. A concave lens diverges and is the myopia correction.

q: The reflecting telescope was first suggested by Galileo and this arrangement is called the Newtonian design.
e: False. The reflecting telescope of Newtonian design was suggested by Newton, not Galileo. Galileo's telescope was a refractor. Name and inventor have to stay together.

q: In the terrestrial telescope a concave lens, instead of a convex lens is used as an eyepiece to produce a final image which is erect.
e: True. A wide objective gathers light and improves resolution. The eyepiece is the lens toward the eye and adds angular magnification. Microscope magnifying power multiplies objective and eyepiece factors.

q: Total reflecting prisms are used in binoculars to reduce the length of the terrestrial telescope.
e: True. Binoculars are a pair of telescopes, one per eye, using total-reflecting 45-45-90 prisms. The prisms fold the path, shorten the tube, and erect the image. A single shared telescope is not a binocular.

q: A binoculars is an optical instrument which consists of a single telescope for both eyes, and those telescopes employ the total reflecting prisms.
e: False. Binoculars are a pair of telescopes, one for each eye, using total-reflecting prisms. A single shared tube is not a binocular. The prisms also erect and shorten the path.

q: Optics is the branch of physics that studies the nature and properties of light.
e: True. A different driver in place of Optics would describe a different law. Optics and branch have to stay with the same process.

q: A laser, acronym for Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation, is a source of a narrow beam of intense, monochromatic, coherent light.
e: False. Laser is Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, not spontaneous. Spontaneous emission is random in phase and direction. Stimulated emission copies the stimulating photon.

q: A laser produces stimulated emission of photons from excited atoms or molecules.
e: True. The beam is coherent, monochromatic, narrow and intense. Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Laser action needs population inversion and stimulated emission; the cavity is two mirrors.

q: Lasers are classified into three main types: gas lasers, solid-state lasers, and fiber lasers.
e: False. The usual three-way split is gas, solid-state, and semiconductor lasers. Fibre lasers are a solid-state family, not a third top-level class in this listing. Pumping and the medium are what define the type.

q: A laser contains three essential elements: laser medium, power supply and optical cavity.
e: True. Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Laser action needs population inversion and a mirror cavity; the beam is coherent and monochromatic. Spontaneous emission is random in phase and is not the laser process.

q: The laser medium is the material emitting the laser beam.
e: True. Spontaneous emission is random in phase and is not the laser process. Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Laser action needs population inversion and a mirror cavity; the beam is coherent and monochromatic.

q: The power supply delivers energy to the laser medium in the form needed to excite it to emit light, a process called focusing.
e: False. Delivering energy to the laser medium so it can emit is pumping, not focusing. Focusing is what lenses do to a beam. Population inversion comes from that pump.

q: The optical cavity concentrates the light to stimulate the emission of laser radiation.
e: True. It travels at the speed of light. Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Laser action needs population inversion and a mirror cavity; the beam is coherent and monochromatic.

q: The optical cavity consists of two highly refractive lenses.
e: False. A laser cavity is two mirrors, one of them partly transmitting, not two highly refractive lenses. The mirrors send the light back through the medium. Lenses may sit outside; they are not the cavity.

q: Two essential processes to initiate a laser action are spontaneous emission and population inversion.
e: False. The two essentials for laser action are stimulated emission and population inversion. Spontaneous emission starts stray photons, but the amplification is stimulated. Random spontaneous light is not the beam.

q: In stimulated emission, the transition occurs when the atom in its excited state interacts with an incident photon at the transition frequency.
e: True. Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Laser action needs population inversion and stimulated emission; the cavity is two mirrors. The beam is coherent, monochromatic, narrow and intense.

q: Atoms undergoing stimulated emission radiate photons of different frequencies in random directions and out of phase with the stimulating radiation.
e: False. Stimulated emission radiates photons of the same frequency, in the same direction, and in phase with the stimulating wave. Random frequencies and phases are spontaneous emission. Coherence is the laser signature.

q: For stimulated emission to occur, a population inversion would be needed.
e: True. Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Laser action needs population inversion and stimulated emission; the cavity is two mirrors. Stimulated emission to occur a population inversion cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Population inversion means the population of the upper level of a transition would have to be higher than that of the lower level.
e: True. Population and inversion have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of Population would describe a different law.

q: One of the unique properties of a laser beam is incoherence, which means that the light waves it contains are out of phase with one another.
e: False. A laser beam is coherent: the waves stay in phase. Incoherence is ordinary lamp light. Monochromaticity and a narrow beam ride with that coherence.

q: A typical beam divergence is around a milliradian.
e: True. A different driver in place of typical would describe a different law. typical and beam have to stay with the same process.

q: Lasers are used in optical fibre communications to send information over large distances.
e: True. An optical fibre guides light in a core by total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary. Incidence must exceed the critical angle or light leaks. Information rides as light pulses, not as copper electrical pulses.

q: Laser range finders are used to determine the chemical composition of an object.
e: False. Laser range finders measure distance from go-and-return time. Chemical composition is spectroscopy, often with a different laser setup. Timing a pulse is not a composition assay.

q: The fibre optics works on the principle of total internal reflection.
e: True. Copper electrical pulses are a different cable. Fibre optics sends information as light pulses in a glass or plastic core, held by total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary. Incidence must exceed the critical angle.

q: Fibre optics refers to the technology that transmits information as electrical pulses along a copper wire.
e: False. Fibre optics sends information as light pulses along a glass or plastic fibre, not as electrical pulses on copper. Copper is ordinary wire. Total internal reflection keeps the light in the core.

q: An optical fibre is composed of two concentric layers, called the core and cladding which surrounds the glass fibre core.
e: True. The protective jacket is outside the cladding, not the other way round. Light is meant to stay in the core. An optical fibre guides light in a core by total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary.

q: The cladding is surrounded by a layer called core which protects the optical fibre.
e: False. The core is inside; the cladding surrounds the core, and a jacket then protects the fibre. Light is guided in the core by bouncing at the core-cladding boundary. The names are not inside-out.

q: The refractive index of core will be slightly greater than that of cladding.
e: True. Light is meant to stay in the core. Cladding surrounds the core and provides the lower refractive index for total internal reflection. The protective jacket is outside the cladding, not the other way round.

q: If the light ray strikes the core to cladding interface at an angle less than the critical angle, it is total internally reflected back into the core.
e: False. Total internal reflection needs an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. Steeper than critical, the ray is TIR-guided. Less than critical, part of the light leaks into the cladding.

q: If the angle of incidence at the core to cladding interface is less than the critical angle, both reflection and refraction take place.
e: True. An echo is reflection, not refraction. Sound still obeys the same bend-toward-the-slower-medium idea as light. Cladding surrounds the core and provides the lower refractive index for total internal reflection.

q: A useful application of fibre optics is in endoscopy.
e: True. Copper electrical pulses are a different cable. Fibre optics sends information as light pulses in a glass or plastic core, held by total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary. Useful application of fibre optics is in cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: In medicine, endoscopy is a surgical procedure to examine the exterior of a solid organ of the human body.
e: False. Endoscopy uses fibre bundles to look inside a hollow organ or cavity, not at the exterior of a solid organ. Light goes in and the image comes back out the same cable. Exterior inspection does not need that fibre path.

q: A spectrometer is a scientific instrument used to separate and measure spectral components of a physical phenomenon.
e: True. Wavelengths then fingerprint the source. A microscope magnifies shape; it does not by itself sort colour this way. A spectrometer separates and measures spectral components, usually with a collimator, a disperser and a telescope.

q: The optical spectrometer consists of light source, collimator, dispersion elements and a microscope.
e: False. An optical spectrometer uses a light source, collimator, dispersing element, and a telescope, not a microscope. The telescope views the spectrum. A microscope is the wrong viewing arm.

q: The collimated beam from a specific light source is dispersed by dispersion element such as prism or grating.
e: True. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium.

q: In a spectrophotometer, dispersion element combines light into a single beam which is allowed to fall on the sample to be investigated.
e: False. In a spectrophotometer the dispersing element splits light into wavelengths; it does not combine them into one beam. Each slice then probes the sample. Combining would undo the spectrum.

q: Three of the most common optical spectrometers are spectrophotometers, spectrofluorometers and Raman spectrometers.
e: True. Wavelengths then fingerprint the source. A microscope magnifies shape; it does not by itself sort colour this way. Three of the most common optical spectrometers cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Photometry is the science of measuring visible light in units that are weighted according to the sensitivity of human eye.
e: True. Main quantities are luminous flux, intensity, luminance and illuminance. Photometry measures visible light with weights matched to the human eye, about 400 nm to 700 nm. Peak eye sensitivity is green near 555 nm.

q: The human eye responds only to light having wavelengths between about $400	ext{ nm}$ and $900	ext{ nm}$.
e: False. The human eye responds from about 400 nm to 700 nm, not out to 900 nm. 900 nm is infrared, which photometry of vision does not count. Green near 555 nm is the peak of that eye curve.

q: Human eye is more sensitive to green light of $555	ext{ nm}$ compared to other colors.
e: True. A different driver in place of Human would describe a different law. Human and eye have to stay with the same process.

q: In photometry, there are three main photometric quantities: luminous flux, luminous intensity, and illuminance.
e: False. Photometry also counts luminance, intensity per unit area in a given direction, as a main quantity. Flux, intensity, luminance, and illuminance are the set. Dropping luminance leaves the candela-per-square-metre idea out.

q: Luminous flux is a measurement of the power of visible light produced by a light source.
e: True. The eye's peak wavelength is why 555 nm is the luminous standard. Luminous flux is the visible-light power of a source, measured in lumen. One lumen is 1/683 watt at 555 nm, not at 400 nm.

q: Luminous flux is measured in lumen ($	ext{lm}$).
e: True. Luminous flux is the visible-light power of a source, measured in lumen. One lumen is 1/683 watt at 555 nm, not at 400 nm. The eye's peak wavelength is why 555 nm is the luminous standard.

q: One lumen is equivalent to $1/683	ext{ watt}$ of light with a wavelength of $400	ext{ nm}$.
e: False. One lumen is 1/683 watt of light at 555 nm, the eye's peak, not at 400 nm. 400 nm is the violet edge where the eye is much less sensitive. That 555 nm choice is why luminous units track vision.

q: Luminous intensity is a measure of the luminous flux emitted by a light source in a direction per unit solid angle.
e: True. Luminous intensity is flux per unit solid angle, I_v = Phi / Omega, in candela. Candela is lumen per steradian. Lux is illuminance, not this candela quantity.

q: Luminous intensity is measured in lux ($	ext{lx}$) or lumen per steradian.
e: False. Luminous intensity is the candela, lumen per steradian, not lux. Lux is illuminance, lumen per square metre. Steradian is a solid angle, not an area.

q: A solid angle is a measure of the amount of the field of view from some particular point that a given object covers.
e: True. In a solid, v = sqrt(Y/rho), Young's modulus over density. Y and the bulk modulus are elasticity properties, unit N m^-2. Liquids use bulk modulus B instead of Y.

q: In SI system, a solid angle is expressed in steradian ($	ext{sr}$).
e: True. In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Work done on the system is negative W in this convention. In a solid, v = sqrt(Y/rho), Young's modulus over density.

q: Luminance is the luminous intensity per unit area of light travelling in a given direction.
e: True. Lux is illuminance, not this candela quantity. Luminous intensity is flux per unit solid angle, I_v = Phi / Omega, in candela. Candela is lumen per steradian.

q: The SI unit for luminance is lux ($	ext{lx}$).
e: False. Luminance's SI unit is candela per square metre. Lux is illuminance on a receiving surface. Mixing those units mixes outgoing brightness with landing light.

q: Illuminance is the total luminous flux incident on a surface per unit area.
e: True. Illuminance is luminous flux landing per unit area, in lux, and follows E_v = I_v cos theta / r^2. It falls as the square of distance. School reading areas are often quoted near 500 lux.

q: The SI unit for illuminance is lux ($	ext{lx}$).
e: True. It falls as the square of distance. School reading areas are often quoted near 500 lux. Illuminance is luminous flux landing per unit area, in lux, and follows E_v = I_v cos theta / r^2.

q: The illuminance at any point on a surface is directly proportional to the square of the distance between the source and surface.
e: False. Illuminance is inversely proportional to the square of the source-to-surface distance. Double r and E_v falls to one quarter. A direct r squared law would brighten a surface as you walked away.
